title: Understand MCP Architecture and Contracts
summary: Use a reproducible local child-process lab to model MCP roles, lifecycle, primitives, authorization, timeout handling, and portable provider boundaries.
objectives: Explain MCP host, client, and server responsibilities without collapsing their trust boundaries.
Trace initialization, protocol-version agreement, capability negotiation, operation, and shutdown.
Distinguish prompts, resources, and tools by who controls them and what risk they introduce.
Design a narrow MCP tool contract with typed inputs, outputs, errors, and human-control points.

sections.title: Start with three roles and one connection per server
paragraphs: An MCP host is the AI application that coordinates user intent, policy, consent, model access, and results from multiple connections. It creates a separate MCP client for each server. Each client maintains its own session, negotiated capabilities, request identifiers, timeout state, and failure boundary. An MCP server exposes focused prompts, resources, or tools. Speaking MCP does not make a local or remote server trusted.

The lab starts two real Node.js child processes named curriculum and assessment. Their lifecycle state, capabilities, drafts, and identities remain separate. Duplicate configured identities and invalid workspace definitions are rejected during initialized-session setup before a child is spawned; an invalid constructor does not leak a child. Unqualified tool-name collisions are resolved as curriculum::create_training_draft and assessment::create_training_draft. The host alone decides whether information may cross those connections.

sections.title: Negotiate before operating
paragraphs: This fixture pins a limited teaching profile to MCP revision 2025-11-25. The client sends initialize with protocolVersion set to 2025-11-25, a capabilities object, and clientInfo. The server returns the agreed version, capabilities, and serverInfo. The client then sends notifications/initialized without an id. It expects no response, and the server does not send an initialized notification. The fixture blocks operations until that client notification arrives.

Initialization evidence applies only to the current session. Missing tools capability means no tool operation, even if configuration names a tool. The lab closes stdin, waits 200 milliseconds, sends SIGTERM if necessary, waits another 200 milliseconds, then sends SIGKILL and waits up to 500 milliseconds. It sends no JSON-RPC shutdown method. These are deterministic fixture values, not production recommendations. The 2025-11-25 pin does not establish compatibility with a later specification revision.

code.label: Pinned initialization and shutdown trace

sections.title: Prompts, resources, and tools have different control models
paragraphs: Prompts are user-controlled templates, resources are application-controlled context, and tools are functions a model may propose. These control labels help describe who initiates selection. They do not authorize an action. Prompt text, resource contents, tool descriptions, and tool results are all untrusted input, even when discovery and schema validation succeed.

In the demo, the prompt description explicitly says it is not authorization. The assessment child cannot use a string saying SERVER SAYS APPROVED to act in the curriculum workspace. The host decides which server and primitives are exposed, what context may be sent, whether confirmation is required, and which trusted executor may perform a side effect.

code.label: Control is separate from authority
code.code:
PROMPT user selects a template
RESOURCE application selects context to read
TOOL model may propose a function call
HOST POLICY checks identity, scope and approval

sections.title: Make tool contracts narrow and inspectable
paragraphs: The demonstrated tool has a stable name, a decision-oriented description, precise string bounds, required fields, and additionalProperties set to false. Its workspace pattern is ^ws_[a-z0-9]{4,12}$. Both ws_aaaa and ws_aaaaaaaa satisfy that pattern. Schema validity therefore proves only shape. Authorization requires exact membership in the host's trusted workspace allowlist.

The protocol-facing tools definition does not contain a hostAuthorizationTuple. That name is nonstandard host policy outside the MCP tools schema. The host separately checks exact server identity, exact tool name, exact workspace membership, title bounds, and an approval value bound to the prior values. The fixture's approvalToken is exactly JSON.stringify(['APPROVE', expectedIdentity, name, workspaceId, title]): four bound values plus the fixed APPROVE sentinel, serialized as exactly five array elements. It is not a cryptographic security token and has no circular fifth token field. A valid call with invalid tool input returns a normal result containing isError:true. A malformed tools/call or unknown tool name returns JSON-RPC error -32602.

A timed-out write has outcome UNKNOWN, not NOT_APPLIED. Do not replay it automatically. The fixture quarantines expired request identifiers in a history bounded to 64 entries and 5,000 milliseconds, prevents a late response from satisfying a new request, and uses a read-only state resource for reconciliation. An unrelated response identifier is a fatal protocol error. Cleanup is awaited so pending requests are rejected and children terminate.

code.label: Protocol tool schema

sections.title: Separate the portable contract from provider adapters
paragraphs: The lab requires Node.js 24 or later and uses only built-in modules and local child processes. It makes no network request and uses no model, provider SDK, credential, remote server, production authentication system, durable store, or production sandbox. Passing the lab therefore does not prove compatibility with a hosted provider, local-model runtime, open-weight model, remote authorization service, or a later MCP revision.

Transfer the design by retaining provider-neutral invariants: one isolated session per server, negotiated capabilities, exact server and workspace identity, allowed tools, approval binding, timeout classification, postcondition checks, reconciliation, and awaited shutdown. Implement each provider or framework integration as a separately tested adapter. Verify its transport, SDK objects, approval surface, error mapping, supported MCP revision, and fallback behavior against dated first-party documentation. Do not infer identical behavior from the shared MCP name.

code.label: Run the runtime suite and learner probe separately
code.code:
cd training/reliable-agent-workflows/mcp-architecture/lab
npm test
npm run learner:test
npm run learner:solution

activity.title: Repair exact workspace authorization in a real child-process flow
instructions: From the repository root, run cd training/reliable-agent-workflows/mcp-architecture/lab. Confirm that Node.js is version 24 or later. Run node src/demo.mjs, save the actual output, and map each output line to the host, one of the two clients, or one of the two child servers.

Run npm test and save its actual result as the full runtime-suite evidence. The suite is expected to contain 23 tests, including collision, invalid-second-definition, bounded64, and unknown-ID cases. Treat the three independent security boundaries as regression-tested cases in this suite. Do not count separate collision, invalid-constructor, or history-bound qualification probes as extra cases, or attribute them to an older 20-case count, unless the repository output explicitly does so.

Run npm run learner:test and save the intentional baseline failure. This command imports test/learner-scope.test.mjs, which imports the editable src/scope-policy.broken.mjs. The prefix policy treats schema-valid ws_aaaaaaaa as allowed because it starts with ws_aaaa. The host call must demonstrate denial and zero server effects, not merely a helper return value.

Edit src/scope-policy.broken.mjs so the function is exactly: export function workspaceAllowed(allowedWorkspaces, requestedWorkspace) { return allowedWorkspaces.includes(requestedWorkspace); }. Rerun npm run learner:test after the edit and save the actual passing result. This rerun imports the edited file and is the proof of the learner's repair. Do not use npm run learner:solution as proof of the edit.

Make a meaningful changed-input assertion in test/learner-scope.test.mjs, or in the test input used by that test. Use the schema-valid but unauthorized identity ws_aaaab while keeping allowedWorkspaces as ['ws_aaaa']. Verify that host.callDraft denies the request and state.drafts.length === 0. Do not change only the requested ID to an authorized value while retaining denial assertions. Rerun the learner test and save the actual one-test passing result.

Run npm test again after the learner edit and save the actual full-regression result. Record the post-repair result as 23 passing tests only if the command output actually reports that result. Confirm that the intentional baseline remains tested independently and that no assertions or security-boundary checks were weakened.

Run npm run learner:solution separately and label its actual two-case result as reference comparison only. It imports src/scope-policy.solution.mjs, not the edited broken file. Its cases should deny ws_aaaaaaaa with zero effects and allow exact ws_aaaa with receipt exercise-ok:1. This result does not prove the learner's edit.

Write a causal explanation covering separate child sessions; initialize and the client-sent initialized notification; primitive control labels; schema validity versus authority; the exact five-element approval serialization; UNKNOWN timeout outcomes and no automatic replay; reconciliation with bounded history; bounded diagnostics; awaited shutdown; and what a provider adapter would still need to test. Explain which observed behavior would change first if the host confused schema validity, discovery, or prompt text with authorization.
evidence: A saved demo transcript from the actual node src/demo.mjs run, with every line annotated as host, client, or one of two isolated child servers.

The actual npm test output, recorded as the full runtime suite. Record 23 tests, including collision, invalid-second-definition, bounded64, and unknown-ID, only when the repository output confirms that count. Keep separate collision, invalid-constructor, and history-bound qualification probes distinct from the suite count. Confirm that the three independent security boundaries remain regression-tested, rather than describing them as only independent probes.

The intentional npm run learner:test baseline failure, followed by the actual passing rerun after editing src/scope-policy.broken.mjs. The saved evidence must distinguish the baseline failure from the repaired-file proof.

A changed-input observation from test/learner-scope.test.mjs showing that schema-valid unauthorized ws_aaaab is denied by host.callDraft and leaves state.drafts.length === 0 while allowedWorkspaces remains ['ws_aaaa'].

The actual post-edit npm test result, saved after the repair and reported as complete regression evidence. Do not claim 23 passing tests unless the command output shows it. Include the unchanged independent intentional-baseline coverage and all three independent security-boundary checks.

A separately labelled npm run learner:solution reference comparison with two actual cases: denial with zero effects for ws_aaaaaaaa and an authorized receipt exercise-ok:1 for exact ws_aaaa. State explicitly that this imports src/scope-policy.solution.mjs and does not prove the learner's edit.

The repaired function text, causal rubric response, and scope limits: credit exact membership, zero unauthorized effects, one authorized reference effect, schema-versus-authority reasoning, lifecycle direction, isolated sessions, exact approval serialization, no replay after UNKNOWN, bounded reconciliation, awaited shutdown, and honest provider-adapter limits. Do not add hosted-model evidence or claim README accuracy without repository evidence.

questions.prompt: Which component should own user consent and coordinate policy across MCP connections?
choices: Any remote server
The host application
The tool result
The JSON schema
questions.explanation: The host coordinates consent, model access, policy, and separate client connections. A result or schema carries data rather than authority.

questions.prompt: A server is configured with a write tool but did not advertise tools capability during initialization. What should happen?
choices: Call the tool because configuration is authoritative
Invent a tools capability for this session
Do not call it; use the declared fallback or fail closed
Send notifications/initialized again
questions.explanation: Negotiated capability state governs the current session. Configuration cannot manufacture support, and repeating initialized does not negotiate a new capability.

questions.prompt: Both ws_aaaa and ws_aaaaaaaa match the workspace schema. What does that establish?
choices: Only that both strings have the permitted shape
That both belong to the caller
That one approval value authorizes both
That either write has already succeeded
questions.explanation: The pattern validates syntax only. Exact trusted-allowlist membership, approval binding, and postcondition evidence are separate checks.

questions.prompt: A write request times out before the host receives a response. What is the safest next step?
choices: Replay it immediately with a new request id
Report success because the schema was valid
Report no effect because no response arrived
Classify the outcome as UNKNOWN and reconcile before any retry
questions.explanation: The child may have applied the write before the timeout. Automatic replay can duplicate the effect, so quarantine the expired id and reconcile state.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible way to transfer this local lab design to several providers?
choices: Assume every MCP product has identical transport and approval behavior
Keep policy invariants provider-neutral and validate each adapter separately
Treat a passing local test as remote authorization evidence
Replace exact scope checks with each provider's tool description
questions.explanation: The local fixture demonstrates architecture and policy invariants, not provider compatibility. Each adapter needs dated first-party verification and integration tests.
